newsitem.title: USA: Second US finance industry reform bill introduced.
newsitem.headline: Second US finance industry reform bill introduced.

text.p: One day after House banking Committee chairman Jim Leach introduced a bill to overhaul the U.S. financial sector, another member of the committee introduced a measure offering a slightly different approach.

Rep Marge Roukema, chairwoman of the Financial Institutions Subcommittee, said her bill would also break down the legal barriers between banks and other financial service firms like securities dealers and insurance companies.
"This legislation represents a concrete effort to break the current logjam that has blocked financial services reform in the past," the New Jersey Republican said Wednesday.
The bill, co-sponsored by Minnesota Republican Rep Bruce Vento, was developed in coordination with a coalition of finance industry trade groups known as the Alliance for Financial Modernization.
The group includes the American Bankers Association, America's Community Bankers, Consumers Bankers, Investment Company Institute, Securities Industry Association, and the Bankers Roundtable.
While all members of the group support the "general approach" of the bill, not all support all of the bill's provisions, Roukema said.
If the bill passed, it would create a new category of holding company -- financial services holding company -- under which companies could choose to organize.

Such a company could own or affiliate with a broad range of companies as long as 75 percent of its business was in financial activities such as banking, insurance, securities dealing, and wholesale finance.
But a holding company would not be allowed to enter the agency insurance business unless it bought an insurance agency that had been in business for at least two years.
Certain securities activities, such as asset-backed securities and municipal revenue bonds, could be offered in a new, separate securities affiliate.

Chairman Leach's bill would allow subsidiaries of existing bank holding companies to engage in securities dealings. Affiliates of bank holding companies could offer insurance as principal, agent or broker.
Both proposals are similiar to measures that were introduced by the two lawmakers last year. Since then, however, bank regulators have taken steps to allow banks to expand into non-banking areas.

On Dec 20, Federal Reserve voted to allow bank subsidiaries to garner a greater share of revenue from underwriting activity. And Wednesday, the Fed proposed abolishing many of the remaining legal barriers separating a bank from its securities dealing unit.
In November, Comptroller of the Currency's office said it would allow nationally-chartered banks to enter an array of non-bank markets.

Analysts have said those moves feed banks to enter othe fields without freeing otehrs to enter banking. That should increase the pressure on Congress to pass comprehensive legislation to level the playing field, they said.
